reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Often presents with painless obstructive jaundice and a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped gland, closely mimicking pancreatic carcinoma
Cross-sectional imaging classically shows diffuse parenchymal swelling with a hypoattenuating rim or capsule-like halo and loss of the normal lobulated contour
Type 1 is the pancreatic manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease, with raised serum IgG4 and frequent involvement of the biliary tree, salivary glands, kidneys, and retroperitoneum
Type 2 (idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis) shows granulocytic epithelial lesions on histology, has normal IgG4, affects younger patients, and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease
A dramatic response to a corticosteroid trial supports the diagnosis, but malignancy must be reasonably excluded before treating
Diagnosis integrates imaging, serology, other organ involvement, histology, and steroid response (as in the HISORt and international consensus criteria)
Type 1 disease relapses commonly, whereas type 2 tends to follow a more benign, non-relapsing course
Management centres on corticosteroid induction, with immunomodulators or rituximab considered for relapsing or refractory type 1 disease
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a corticosteroid-responsive fibroinflammatory disorder of the pancreas. In type 1 disease the pancreas is one target organ of systemic IgG4-related disease, in which an aberrant immune response drives infiltration by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, producing diffuse glandular swelling and a peripheral rim of oedema and fibrosis. Type 2 disease is confined to the pancreas and is characterised histologically by neutrophilic infiltration of the duct epithelium (granulocytic epithelial lesions) without the raised IgG4 or multi-organ features of type 1. Both forms compress the pancreatic and intrapancreatic bile ducts, causing strictures, obstructive jaundice, and secondary exocrine impairment, and both typically regress with immunosuppression.
additionalDifferentials: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with a dominant stricture
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI with MRCP to assess parenchymal swelling, the capsule-like rim, and duct strictures
Serum IgG4 and total IgG with subclass analysis
Endoscopic ultrasound with core or fine-needle biopsy for histology when malignancy is a concern
Assessment for other organ involvement (biliary, salivary, renal, retroperitoneal)
Serum CA 19-9 to help weigh the likelihood of adenocarcinoma
Documentation of response to a defined corticosteroid trial
Faecal elastase to gauge exocrine insufficiency
redFlags: A discrete focal mass, upstream duct dilatation, or vascular encasement suggesting carcinoma rather than autoimmune pancreatitis
Markedly elevated CA 19-9 or progressive weight loss
Failure to respond to an adequate corticosteroid trial
New or worsening jaundice during treatment
Development of a dominant biliary stricture raising concern for cholangiocarcinoma
reference.prognosis: Both subtypes usually respond promptly and completely to corticosteroids, with resolution of jaundice and normalisation of gland size; type 1 disease relapses in a substantial proportion of patients and may need maintenance immunosuppression, whereas type 2 rarely relapses. Long-standing or recurrent disease can lead to pancreatic atrophy with exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing a focal mass-forming case as adenocarcinoma, or vice versa, leading to unnecessary resection or delayed cancer treatment
Treating with steroids before reasonably excluding malignancy
Relying on a normal serum IgG4, which does not exclude the diagnosis and may be normal in type 2 disease
Overlooking associated biliary, renal, or salivary involvement that supports systemic IgG4-related disease
Failing to monitor type 1 patients for relapse after tapering therapy
